[2 URLs → 1 origin: the Series H announcement](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/28/anthropic-open-ai-startup-value.html). 'Close to $1 trillion' fits $965B.

evidence: Compiled revenue timelines (VentureBeat, Sacra) put Anthropic's annualized run-rate at roughly $1B around Dec 2024–Jan 2025, consistent with 'low single billions.' A company-disclosed metric with no independent audit — tier-4 ceiling, capped at plausible even though the trajectory is consistently reported.

[2 URLs → 1 origin: Anthropic's own investor disclosure](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/28/anthropic-open-ai-startup-value.html) — self-reported revenue metric, tier-4 ceiling applies regardless of how widely repeated.

claim: Third-party trackers put Anthropic's annualized revenue at around [$74 billion] as of [late July 2026] [03:10]

These are analyst estimation firms, not Anthropic's own disclosure, so not tier-4 capped. [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/anthropic-openai-revenue).

claim: Anthropic's month-over-month revenue growth rate fell from roughly [51%] in [May 2026] to roughly [8%] by [July 2026] [03:10–04:13]

evidence: Epoch AI's tracking describes month-over-month growth cooling 'from roughly 55% in the spring to the mid-single digits by July' — directionally matches the claimed 51%→8% deceleration, though exact figures vary by tracker and rounding. Built partly on self-reported ($47B) and partly on third-party-tracked numbers, so plausible rather than confirmed.

claim: Somewhere between [$3 trillion and $4 trillion] has reportedly already been poured into the American AI industry (data centers, chips, power deals) [06:19]
quote: somewhere between three and four trillion dollars has reportedly been poured into the American AI industry, data centers, chips, power deals, the lot.
evidence: The $3–4T figures in circulation (Morgan Stanley/Moody's '$3T or more in the coming years', JPMorgan '>$5T', Jensen Huang '$3–4T by decade's end') are forward projections of the total eventual build-out, not money already spent. Actual cumulative hyperscaler capex to date is much smaller: ~$250B (2024) + ~$410B (2025) + ~$725B guided (2026) ≈ $1.4T for the big four alone, and economy-wide totals are still well under $3T. The claim presents a future total as money already 'poured in.' [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-02/the-3-trillion-ai-data-center-build-out-spurs-a-debt-market-boom).

claim: The majority of the money poured into the American AI industry is reportedly debt — corporate bonds, borrowed money [06:19]
quote: the majority of it is reportedly debt, corporate bonds, borrowed money.
evidence: FactSet: incremental debt was 9% of hyperscaler capex in FY24, rising to 32% LTM by mid-2026 — fast-growing, but far from a majority. Total AI-tied debt reached ~$1.2T by Oct 2025 against a total build-out estimated at $3–5T+, roughly a quarter to a third. Equity (Alphabet's $84.75B raise, hyperscalers' own cash flow) still supplies most of the funding. Debt is a fast-growing minority share, not the majority. [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://insight.factset.com/hyperscalers-tap-external-financing-as-ai-capex-outruns-cash-flow).

claim: Interest on roughly [$2–3 trillion] of AI industry debt at a 'perfectly normal' corporate bond rate of [3–4%] costs the industry about [$100 billion] a year [06:19–07:22]
quote: On two to three trillion dollars of debt at a perfectly normal corporate bond rate of three to four percent, the interest alone works out to roughly 100 billion dollars a year
evidence: Both inputs run the same direction as claim 7's error: total AI-tied debt is closer to $1.2–1.5T than $2–3T, while actual yields on AI/data-center investment-grade debt in 2026 run 5–7.5% (QTS Realty 7.23%, a BlackRock-backed Texas data-center deal 7.53%, broad IG index ~5.0–5.5%) — not the 3–4% called 'perfectly normal.' The arithmetic on the stated inputs is correct, but the inputs themselves don't match current reporting: debt overstated, rate understated. [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://finance.biggo.com/news/96a7d7dc-1050-4775-af2b-170a13d96e98).

claim: Most of the big AI labs reportedly lose money on every single request served [07:22]
quote: most of the big labs reportedly lose money on every single request served.
evidence: OpenAI is confirmed unprofitable on inference (projected to burn $14B in 2026, gross margin down to 33%). But Anthropic — this video's own subject — has reportedly moved the other way: inference gross margins rose from 38% to over 70% through 2025–2026, even though overall net profitability stays negative (R&D/training costs, not per-query costs, are the drag). 'Most labs lose money on every request' overstates a pattern that's already reversing for at least one major lab.

claim: The US white-collar wage economy is roughly [$10 trillion] [08:25]
quote: the roughly 10 trillion-dollar white-collar wage economy
evidence: No single source gives an exact 'white-collar wage economy' total. Total US wages across all occupations were $12.3T (BLS, 2025); one AI-exposure study puts $3.7T in wages specifically in the highest-AI-exposure occupations (59.9M jobs). $10T for the broader white-collar segment (a majority of the $12.3T total) is a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate, not a directly sourced figure. [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://www.bls.gov/cew/publications/employment-and-wages-annual-averages/current/).

claim: AI lab leaders like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have spent years publicly predicting that huge swaths of white-collar jobs will simply vanish [08:25]

claim: Chinese open AI models are, by most measures, slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of the best American AI systems [10:30]
quote: Chinese labs with a fraction of America's computing power have produced open models that are by most measures slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of the best American systems.
evidence: 2026 benchmarks show Chinese open models trading blows with closed frontier models: DeepSeek V4-Pro hits 80.6% on SWE-Bench Verified, Qwen3-Max scores 90.5 on Arena-Hard versus Claude Sonnet 4.6's 86.4, and Kimi K2 Thinking ranks as the strongest open model outside OpenAI/Google/Anthropic. claim: Chinese open models now reportedly account for more than [60%] of all tokens used by American firms, per OpenRouter data [11:32]
quote: according to data from OpenRouter, which routes AI traffic worldwide, Chinese open models now reportedly account for more than 60% of all tokens used by American firms.
evidence: A 61% figure is real but traces to a single week in February 2026, measured only among OpenRouter's top-10 most-used models — not 'all tokens' and not specifically 'American firms.' Broader, more current OpenRouter-based measures show Chinese-origin models at 46.4% of routed tokens by June 2026 (vs 35.7% US-origin), up from under 1.2% in late 2024. Real and dramatic share gain, but 'more than 60%' cherry-picks the narrowest, most-dated snapshot rather than the current broader figure (mid-40s%). [2 URLs → 2 origins](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/chinese-ai-models-now-capture-020440715.html).

claim: A recent survey of thousands of companies reportedly found that over [70%] of the AI customer service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications [14:41]
quote: A recent survey of thousands of companies reportedly found that over 70% of the AI customer service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications.
evidence: Matches a real May 2026 Sinch-commissioned survey of 2,527 senior decision-makers: 74% of enterprises rolled back an AI customer communications agent. Two caveats cap this at plausible: Sinch is a CPaaS/customer-engagement vendor with a commercial stake in this narrative — an interested party, tier-4 ceiling regardless of syndication — and the survey measures the share of enterprises reporting at least one rollback, not the share of deployed agents rolled back, a subtly different number than stated.

claim: Across the whole economy, the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at something under [100,000] workers a year [14:41]
quote: the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at something under 100,000 workers a year.
evidence: Challenger, Gray & Christmas' AI-attributed layoff tracker counted 54,836 US job cuts for full-year 2025 — under 100,000, matching the claim for the most recently completed year. But 2026 was already at 87,714 AI-attributed cuts by end of May, tracking to exceed 100,000 for the full year, so the claim held for 2025 but was likely already stale by this video's July 2026 publication. Other cited estimates (Goldman Sachs ~16,000/month ≈ 190,000/yr net) run well above 100,000, so 'most optimistic' is doing real work here.
